prayer.text: Saint Elizabeth of Portugal, pray for us.

cues.text: A Pious Aragonese Princess
Born in 1271 as a daughter of King Pedro III of Aragon, Elizabeth was named for her great-aunt St. Elizabeth of Hungary .

Known in Portugal by the Spanish form Isabel, she was raised with striking religious discipline from childhood, reciting the full Divine Office daily and practicing regular fasting and penance well before her marriage.
A Difficult Royal Marriage
Married young to King Diniz of Portugal , Elizabeth maintained her own regular devotions and quiet charity toward the poor and sick.
He was a capable, hard-working ruler known as the 'working king', but notoriously unfaithful in his personal life.
Her goodness made the court uncomfortable for many around her.
Rather than confront her husband's infidelities with bitterness, she worked patiently, through gentleness and forbearance, to win his eventual reform.
Riding Between Armies
Elizabeth's gift for reconciling bitter conflicts became legendary during her own lifetime.
In 1323, her son Afonso rebelled against his father Diniz over favoritism shown to the king's illegitimate children.
War seemed certain — until Elizabeth rode in person between the two armies and negotiated a reconciliation between husband and son.
A Widow's Retirement
After Diniz's death in 1325, Elizabeth retired to a convent of Poor Clares she had founded at Coimbra .
Taking the Franciscan Tertiary habit, she devoted herself to prayer and service to the poor and sick.
This was the retirement she had long desired, now finally free of the demands of court.
A Final Mission of Peace

In 1336, now in her sixties, Elizabeth was called from her retirement one final time when her son, now King Afonso IV, marched troops against the King of Castile over his mistreatment of Elizabeth's granddaughter.

Despite her age and failing strength, the queen dowager hurried to the armies gathered at Estremoz and once again negotiated a peaceful settlement — an effort that, however, brought on the fever from which she died on July 4, 1336.
Legacy
Elizabeth was buried at her beloved convent in Coimbra, where her body was later found remarkably incorrupt, examined and confirmed as such by medical and Church authorities as recently as 1912.
Canonized by Pope Urban VIII in 1625, she remains honored as 'the Peacemaker,' a queen whose royal power was consistently placed in service of reconciliation rather than conquest.
